title: Afghanistan is starving and the world is looking away
gist: The WFP's Afghanistan country director describes a collapsing humanitarian supply chain—driven by a closed Pakistan border, a severed Strait of Hormuz route after bombs fell on Iran in February 2026, and an 88%-underfunded programme after UK aid cuts—that is already causing child deaths from malnutrition.

insights.claim: The World Food Programme's Afghanistan operation is only 12 per cent funded, according to its country director, forcing the organisation to turn away everyone seeking help at its nutrition clinics for the past three months.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: An 88% funding gap in an active famine-risk country is a concrete, quantifiable humanitarian crisis indicator relevant to NGO funding flows, UK/international aid budget debates, and regional stability risk.
insights.quote: WFP’s Afghanistan programme is now only 12 per cent funded
insights.locator: To add to the complexities of geopolitics

insights.claim: Recent cuts to the UK aid budget have caused a further 39 per cent reduction in British support to the WFP's Afghanistan programme, despite the UK historically being a stalwart supporter, forcing WFP to close its famine-prevention programme.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified causal link between a UK domestic fiscal decision (aid budget cuts) and the shutdown of a named famine-prevention programme abroad—directly relevant to tracking UK ODA policy impact and to any NGO/aid-sector funding analysis.
insights.locator: The recent announcement about cuts to the UK aid budget

insights.claim: The author states plainly that children in Afghanistan are already dying as a result of aid funding cuts, and warns that WFP is bracing for a further increase in child mortality in the coming months.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: A direct forward-looking claim from an operational insider that child mortality in Afghanistan will worsen imminently—an actionable early-warning signal for humanitarian and diplomatic response planning.
insights.quote: There is no doubt about it: children in Afghanistan are already dying as a result of aid cuts.

themes.theme: Broken supply chains: Pakistan border and the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: The economy of Afghanistan has stagnated amid drought, earthquakes and flash floods, driving more than 12 million people into acute hunger even before the most recent supply-chain shocks.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: Establishes the pre-existing scale of Afghanistan's humanitarian crisis (12m+ in acute hunger) as the baseline against which subsequent supply disruptions compounded the emergency.
insights.locator: I arrived at a time when Afghanistan was facing the highest levels of malnutrition ever recorded

insights.claim: When the Pakistan-Afghanistan border closed in October 2025, 10,000 tonnes of specialised nutritious food—enough to have fed 1.1 million children—was left stranded and unable to cross.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: Quantifies the direct humanitarian cost of the Pakistan border closure (1.1m children's food supply stranded), a concrete metric for assessing the impact of Pakistan-Afghanistan border policy on regional food security.
insights.locator: When the Pakistan border closed in October 2025

insights.claim: After the Pakistan border closed, WFP rerouted supplies via the port of Karachi through the Strait of Hormuz to Dubai and moved two shipments successfully, but this route was also cut off after 'the first bombs fell on Iran' in February 2026.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: A first-person operational account confirming a February 2026 military strike on Iran disrupted Strait of Hormuz shipping with direct, immediate humanitarian supply-chain consequences well beyond oil markets—relevant to broader geopolitical risk assessment of any Iran conflict's spillover effects on regional logistics.
insights.locator: We managed to move two shipments before the first bombs fell on Iran

insights.claim: After both the Pakistan border and the Strait of Hormuz route were cut off, WFP had no choice but to reroute aid to Afghanistan through nine countries via Central Asia and across the Caspian Sea, adding delays of up to three months.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: Illustrates the fragility of Afghanistan's landlocked logistics network: loss of two chokepoints (Pakistan border, Hormuz) forced a nine-country reroute with three-month delays, a case study in supply-chain resilience failure under geopolitical shock.
insights.locator: There was no choice but to move our aid through nine countries

insights.claim: WFP's Afghanistan hotline, which receives around 140,000 calls a year, saw a 60 per cent rise in distress calls from Afghan women between June and December of the prior year, with many contemplating suicide.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: A quantified, real-time distress indicator (60% rise in hotline calls) that functions as a leading humanitarian-crisis metric, useful for tracking deterioration in Afghan household welfare in near real time.
insights.locator: From June to December last year, we saw a 60 per cent rise

insights.claim: A WFP hotline operator spoke with a woman who, unable to feed her children despite skipping her own meals, had made the decision with her husband to sell their 12-year-old daughter into early marriage to a 40-year-old man known to have a drug addiction.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: A specific, harrowing case illustrating that acute hunger in Afghanistan is driving extreme coping mechanisms including child marriage—evidence for the depth of the crisis beyond aggregate statistics.
insights.locator: One of our operators spoke to a woman

insights.claim: WFP received a call from an Afghan father who had sold his own kidney in order to put food on the table for his family—a level of desperation the organisation says it has never witnessed before.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: Another concrete extreme-coping data point underscoring the severity of the current crisis relative to WFP's historical experience in Afghanistan.
insights.quote: We recently received a call from a father who had sold his kidney to put food on the table.
insights.locator: It is not only women who call us

insights.claim: Afghanistan is experiencing an increase in extreme weather events, including flash floods that recently killed dozens of people and destroyed entire villages in Nuristan province, and a drought in the west where five young men were found dead after running out of water.
insights.speaker: John Aylieff
insights.so_what: Documents climate-driven mortality events compounding the funding and supply-chain crisis, relevant to assessing overlapping climate and humanitarian risk in Afghanistan.
insights.locator: A few weeks ago, torrential rains and flash floods killed dozens
